name: Dusty sepia
lede: Dusty sepia renders Rikyūcha (利休茶), a traditional Japanese name meaning "Sen no Rikyū's tea", after the tea master whose austere aesthetic favored muted browns.

sections.title: Named for a tea master
sections.body:
Our color library gives the source as 利休茶 (Rikyūcha), "Sen no Rikyū's tea": Sen no Rikyū was the sixteenth-century tea master credited with shaping the wabi-sabi aesthetic, and cha here is both the color word for brown and the tea itself [1]. No first-recorded date survives in our sources, so when the name entered use is undocumented here [1]. The library separately notes that the ISCC-NBS 1955 centroid block for this hue groups English dictionary names including Sable, dated by Maerz and Paul to 1892 [2].

The nearest named color in our graph is [[raw-umber]], at a color distance (ΔE2000) of 3.3, almost the same shade; [[sepia]] itself sits 3.8 away and reads more vivid [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this brown in 3,228 of 23,781 paintings, about 13.6 percent, one of the most frequent colors we have matched, as photographed [4]. It peaks in the 1270s (29 of 48 paintings from that decade) at over four times the overall rate, and is strongest in Chinese and Japanese landscape and figure painting going back to the tenth century [4]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the match is computed, not a pigment identification [4].
